note: Sizes are measured by tools/report-sizes.mjs from a real `vite build` (raw / gzip / brotli), attributed per library chunk. criticalPath is what a first visit actually downloads.

libraries.name: GSAP + ScrollTrigger
libraries.role: Scroll orchestration: hero intro timeline, heading reveals, scrubbed timeline progress, counters, velocity-reactive marquee, background parallax.
libraries.why: The only library here that combines a timeline sequencer, a scroll scrubber and a batching helper in one API. ScrollTrigger's `batch()` replaced ~60 lines of IntersectionObserver bookkeeping.

libraries.name: Lenis
libraries.role: Inertial smooth scrolling for the whole document, driven by the GSAP ticker so both share one rAF loop.
libraries.why: Transforms how expensive the site feels. Roughly 3 KB gzipped for a site-wide quality jump; GSAP's ticker integration means zero extra rAF loops.

libraries.name: SplitType
libraries.role: Splits the hero headline and every section title into lines and words so GSAP can mask-reveal them.
libraries.why: Small, dependency-free and predictable. The one caveat is accessibility — `src/lib/split.js` wraps it to put `aria-label` on the container and `aria-hidden` on the fragments.

libraries.name: three.js
libraries.role: Hero background: a full-bleed GLSL shader plane (domain-warped fBm aurora) plus a 3D point constellation with damped pointer parallax.
libraries.why: By far the largest dependency and the single biggest visual upgrade. Justified here only because the hero is the whole first impression; it is lazily imported and suspended when off-screen. A lighter site should use the 2D canvas fallback that ships alongside it.

libraries.name: Motion (motion.dev)
libraries.role: Spring physics for UI: the sliding nav indicator, mobile menu open/close, cursor spotlight, card tilt, magnetic buttons and chip pops.
libraries.why: Deliberately scoped to short, retargetable UI springs. GSAP handles anything with a timeline or a scroll position; Motion handles 'make this feel physical'. Splitting the two avoided re-implementing spring physics on top of GSAP.

libraries.name: anime.js
libraries.role: The agent-architecture diagram: path drawing via `svg.createDrawable`, traffic dots via `svg.createMotionPath`, and a `scrambleText` decode on the label.
libraries.why: For pure SVG work anime.js v4 is the shortest path — DrawSVG and MotionPath equivalents are built in rather than plugins. Interpolating colour and SVG attributes 'just works'.

libraries.name: tsParticles (hand-composed)
libraries.role: The interactive particle network behind the contact card: pointer linking, click-to-push, automatic blur/off-screen pausing.
libraries.why: Right tool for the contact card, wrong tool for the hero — a declarative config replaced ~150 lines of bespoke canvas. The convenience preset is not used: the engine is composed from @tsparticles/basic plus three interactions, which drops emoji/image/line/polygon/square/star shapes and nine interactions this site never touches, cutting it from 45.0 to 30.8 KB gzip. Composing by hand means loading @tsparticles/plugin-interactivity yourself — loadBasic does not, and without it every interaction silently no-ops.

libraries.name: Lottie (lottie_light)
libraries.role: The animated 'agent core' badge in the hero profile card.
libraries.why: The `lottie_light` build is imported rather than the full player, because the only thing that separates them is the expression engine — which this site never uses and which is the sole reason the full build needs `eval`. That took it from 77.6 to 45.8 KB gzip and removed the eval warning. The 16 KB asset is generated programmatically for this site, so licensing is clean; hand-authoring is only realistic for simple shapes, and anything designer-grade needs After Effects + Bodymovin.

libraries.name: Rive (@rive-app/canvas)
libraries.role: Wired up and demoed on the lab page with an MIT-licensed .riv; not shipped on the main page.
libraries.why: The runtime is MIT, needs no attribution, and its player beats Lottie's. The blocker is the ASSET, not the code: `.riv` is a compiled binary that only the Rive editor can produce, and *exporting* one requires a paid plan (Cadet, ~$9/seat/mo). You can play any `.riv` for free, which is what the lab does with the MIT-licensed rating.riv from rive-app/rive-react. It is absent from the main page because a star-rating widget says nothing about AI engineering — not because it is unusable.

libraries.name: AutoAnimate
libraries.role: FLIP animation for the capability grid when the filter chips change what is rendered.
libraries.why: Tiny, and it solved a problem nothing else in the stack addressed: the grid reflows because of a click, not a timeline, so AutoAnimate just watches the parent and interpolates the layout diff. It earned its place by making the filter interaction real rather than decorative.
